title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
authors: Aravindan Kamatchi Sundaram, B. Pabitramohan Prusty, Rohit Batra
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

infographic.key_insight: This review traces how materials literature mining has evolved from rule-based pipelines to LLMs and agentic systems that extract information from text, tables, and figures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated extraction can populate materials databases and knowledge graphs, support research assistants, and enable closed-loop discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories.
method: Review rule-based, NLP, transformer-encoder, and LLM-based extraction approaches.
Assess generated datasets, extraction accuracy, computational costs, and methodological trade-offs.
Outline practical guidelines for reliable, scalable materials data extraction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a review of datasets and evaluation practices, but reports no quantitative results and highlights a shortage of reliable benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable sample-level linking of structure, properties, processing, and performance remains challenging, especially with non-standard terminology across document modalities.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models

title: Machine Learning-Enabled Wireless Power Transfer: A Task-Oriented Review of Structural Optimization, State and Parameter Estimation, and Adaptive Control
authors: Denghao Luo, Yiheng Jiang, Jiaqi Zhao, Yuan Gao, Changsong Cai, Weiyi Huang
abstract: Wireless power transfer (WPT) systems must maintain efficient and safe energy delivery under variations in geometry, coupling, load, alignment, and operating conditions. Machine-learning methods are increasingly applied to accelerate structural design, estimate operating parameters and states, and support adaptive control and scheduling. This review develops a task-oriented framework organized around three interconnected domains: structural design and optimization, parameter and state estimation, and control and optimization. Supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and hybrid or physics-informed methods are compared in terms of data requirements, dependence on physical models, information sources, computational requirements, accuracy, online response, application scope, and optimization objectives. Supervised learning provides rapid surrogate modeling, regression, and classification when representative labeled data are available. Reinforcement learning addresses sequential control and scheduling but introduces challenges in reward design, safe exploration, and simulation-to-reality transfer. Hybrid methods integrate physical knowledge with data-driven models to improve data efficiency and physical consistency. The principal barriers to engineering deployment include limited and biased datasets, weak out-of-distribution generalization, insufficient physical consistency, unsafe online adaptation, embedded-resource constraints, and the absence of standardized benchmarks. Future research should prioritize uncertainty-aware and physics-informed learning, safe simulation-to-reality transfer, lightweight edge deployment, distributed coordination, reproducible evaluation, and digital-twin-assisted development.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning supports wireless power transfer through three connected tasks: structural optimization, state and parameter estimation, and adaptive control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These approaches can help maintain efficient, safe power delivery as geometry, coupling, load, and alignment change.
method: Supervised learning enables fast surrogate models, regression, and classification.
Reinforcement learning addresses sequential control and scheduling.
Hybrid and physics-informed methods combine physical knowledge with data-driven models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract provides a qualitative comparison of learning approaches and identifies limited, biased datasets and missing standardized benchmarks, without reporting quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Engineering deployment requires validation of generalization and safety under unseen operating conditions, especially during online adaptation.
infographic.paper_title: Machine Learning-Enabled Wireless Power Transfer: A Task-Oriented Review of Structural Optimization, State and Parameter Estimation, and Adaptive Control

title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
authors: Chengxi Li, Hanlin Wu, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Jingjing Liu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.

infographic.key_insight: EPIC constrains cumulative prefix probability ratios rather than individual token ratios, directly targeting policy drift across autoregressive generation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: EPIC offers a PPO-style approach for off-policy LLM reinforcement learning that regulates prefix-level drift without requiring expert-routing replay.
method: Model autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon MDP and derive prefix importance weights under behavior-policy sampling.
Use the exact reverse-KL coordinate r − 1 − log(r), whose behavior-policy expectation equals the prefix-distribution KL.
Construct a prefix-level trust region and PPO-style sequence-clipping objective.
infographic.evidence_signal: In off-policy RL experiments with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model, EPIC consistently outperformed standard and sequence-level clipping baselines on mathematical-reasoning benchmarks and remained competitive with routing-replay alternatives.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative gains, and generalization beyond the tested sparse mixture-of-experts model and mathematical-reasoning setting remains unclear.
infographic.paper_title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
authors: Sudipta Paul, Pengrui Quan, Aounon Kumar, Nicholas Tzou, Vivek Kulkarni, Srinivas Chappidi
abstract: Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit-outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent's highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants' final performance with 2x-4x fewer evaluation budget.

infographic.key_insight: HGM-Dual improves long-horizon planning agents by using edit histories and constraint-violation diagnostics to guide harness optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can improve prompts, tools, and workflows around frozen or closed-source LLMs while reducing evaluation costs.
method: Track ancestor edits, behavioral gains, regressions, and ineffective changes in lineage-aware context.
Generate a general child for open-ended exploration from each selected parent.
Generate specialized children targeting harness components linked to the parent's highest-ranked constraint violations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports up to 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy over the strongest baseline and matching HGM variants' final performance with 2–4× fewer evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Targeted edits depend on reliable violation diagnostics; the abstract does not specify benchmarks or diagnostic overhead.
infographic.paper_title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning

title: CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents
authors: Wenhao Yu, Zhengcheng Wang, Jiahong Liu, Zexuan Qiu, Minda Hu, Shaohang Wei
abstract: Joint reinforcement learning and self-distillation combines task rewards with dense teacher guidance for agent training, but their gradients can partly cancel. A mixing coefficient controls relative scale without selectively removing opposing components. We present CORD, a general framework for conflict-aware optimization of two objectives. CORD separates the choice of protected objective from the condition that triggers projection, and combines the gradients once per optimizer mini-batch. A nearest-point formulation yields a closed-form update and characterizes its first-order effect on the protected objective before optimizer transformations. Gradient diagnostics connect conflict in agent training to lost local optimization progress and motivate selective correction. As a gradient-combination mechanism, CORD can be added to different joint training recipes while retaining their objectives. Across three such recipes, it improves ALFWorld success by 1.5-15.9 percentage points. On WebShop, it improves two of the three pairs, with SDAR rising from 60.7% to 64.6% success. Our analyses explain why protection direction and projection gate must be chosen together, and why the distillation objective and its mixing weight remain consequential after projection.

infographic.key_insight: CORD selectively removes conflicting gradient components when combining reinforcement learning and self-distillation, rather than relying on a mixing weight alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CORD can be added to different joint-training recipes without changing their objectives, combining gradients once per optimizer mini-batch.
method: Choose which objective to protect independently of the condition that triggers projection.
Use a nearest-point formulation to obtain a closed-form gradient update.
Characterize the update’s first-order effect on the protected objective before optimizer transformations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three training recipes, CORD improves ALFWorld success by 1.5–15.9 percentage points; on WebShop, it improves two of three pairs, including SDAR from 60.7% to 64.6%.
infographic.watch_item: Protection direction and projection gate must be chosen together; distillation design and mixing weight still matter, and the first-order characterization precedes optimizer transformations.
infographic.paper_title: CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents

title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
authors: Likui Zhang, Zhe Zhu, Zhihao Zhan, Yibo Bai, Hanlin Wang, Dongwei Li
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

infographic.key_insight: AtomicRL improves long-horizon robotic manipulation by aligning reinforcement learning credit assignment and exploration with atomic subtasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a way to post-train vision-language-action policies for multistep manipulation and transfer simulation-trained improvements to physical robots.
method: Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization gates failed-subtask TD residuals at task boundaries while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping.
Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration adjusts task sampling and local exploration incentives according to subtask mastery.
A Real2Sim2Real pipeline connects online reinforcement learning in simulation with real-world deployment.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports absolute gains over PPO of 3.6 and 4.0 percentage points on LIBERO-LONG across two VLA architectures, up to 9.5 points on CALVIN ABC-D, and an average 21.3% real-world improvement with Real2Sim2Real.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment depends on identifying reliable atomic task boundaries and mastery signals; the abstract does not quantify this implementation burden.
infographic.paper_title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation

title: Orbitol: Crystal Generation on Wyckoff Orbits
authors: Ivan Žugec, Joshua Rosenthal, Ivor Lončarić, Jan-Willem van de Meent, Tin Hadži Veljković
abstract: Generative models propose crystalline materials by learning composition and geometry, but unconditional sampling gives no direct control over the space group, which constrains whether responses such as piezoelectricity are symmetry-allowed. We present Orbitol, a crystal generator built on the Crystalite diffusion Transformer that replaces atom tokens with Wyckoff-orbit tokens. Given a space group and a collection of occupied Wyckoff positions, Orbitol generates the atom type and free coordinates of each orbit together with a compatible lattice, so every valid structure is invariant under the operations of the requested group. It generates structures two to three orders of magnitude faster than the symmetry-aware baselines at the evaluated settings. On MP-20, 13.8% of Orbitol's attempts yielded stable or metastable, unique and novel structures that retained the requested space group after relaxation, compared with 10.8% for SGFM, the next best model. We also introduce SPARC, a score that combines retention of the raw detected space group with agreement between the retained-group and training distributions. Finally, we used Orbitol to generate candidates in piezoelectric crystal classes. Of the structures selected by internal screening, 89% passed our density functional theory checks, and 79% also matched no Materials Project or Alexandria entry with the same space group. Their median figure of merit was nine times that of the piezoelectric materials computed in the Materials Project, and 24% of the new candidates ranked in that set's top 10%.

infographic.key_insight: Orbitol generates crystals using Wyckoff-orbit tokens, explicitly controlling space-group symmetry while sampling chemistry, coordinates and lattice geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry-controlled generation can target crystal classes that permit useful responses such as piezoelectricity, narrowing materials screening toward functional candidates.
method: Replace atom tokens in the Crystalite diffusion Transformer with Wyckoff-orbit tokens.
Condition on a space group and occupied Wyckoff positions to generate atom types, free coordinates and a compatible lattice.
Evaluate symmetry retention and distribution agreement with the proposed SPARC score.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MP-20, 13.8% of attempts produced stable or metastable, unique, novel crystals retaining the requested symmetry after relaxation, versus 10.8% for SGFM; generation was 100–1,000× faster than symmetry-aware baselines at evaluated settings.
infographic.watch_item: Symmetry by construction does not guarantee retention after relaxation or physical viability; the reported 89% DFT pass rate applies only to internally screened piezoelectric candidates.
infographic.paper_title: Orbitol: Crystal Generation on Wyckoff Orbits

title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
authors: Nithin Sivakumaran, Ali Payani, Hyunji Lee, Mohit Bansal, Elias Stengel-Eskin
abstract: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.

infographic.key_insight: ToM2Vec uses continuous latent tokens to represent possible partner states, improving multi-agent coordination beyond text-based theory-of-mind reasoning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a compact mechanism for conditioning agents’ decisions on inferred partner beliefs and intentions, including when interacting with unseen partner model families.
method: Learn a fixed budget of continuous theory-of-mind tokens in latent space.
Supervise tokens during training using the partner’s actual thoughts.
Generate tokens at test time to condition each agent’s thoughts and actions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five environments spanning collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive interactions, the abstract reports consistent gains over base and baseline models, weaker performance with text reasoning, and transfer to unseen partner models.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires access to partner thoughts for supervision; the abstract does not quantify performance gains or computational overhead.
infographic.paper_title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination

title: GuideEvolve: Self-Evolving Agent Framework with Expert Guidance and 3Ts Mechanisms
authors: Meihong Jia, Yasemin Timar, Jonathan Taws
abstract: This study introduces GuideEvolve, a self-evolving agent framework incorporating expert guidance and three autonomous regulatory mechanisms, collectively termed the 3Ts: Think Fast and Slow, Throwback, and Termination by choice. The framework addresses critical limitations in extant self-evolving agent paradigms through dual innovations: (1) a task-specific expert-evaluation-driven evolutionary pipeline, and (2) the integration of 3Ts mechanisms to facilitate cognitive optimization, performance recovery via temporal rollback, and adaptive termination protocols. Empirical validation across the MGSM and MMLU benchmarks demonstrates that GuideEvolve attains performance metrics comparable to current state-of-the-art models (89.8% accuracy versus Gödel Agent's 90.6% on MGSM; 89.1% versus 87.9% on MMLU), while exhibiting notably reduced variance (25-59%) and enhanced robustness. Furthermore, the framework achieves a 100% evolution success rate, superior to the baseline's 82%, diminishes required optimization iterations by approximately 50% (from 30 iterations in baseline to 15.1 and 13.4 across tasks), and provides improved stability for production deployment.

infographic.key_insight: GuideEvolve combines expert-guided agent evolution with three self-regulation mechanisms to improve reliability while maintaining competitive benchmark accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More consistent evolution and fewer optimization iterations could make self-evolving agents easier to operate in production.
method: Use task-specific expert evaluation to guide agent evolution.
Apply Think Fast and Slow for cognitive optimization and Throwback for temporal rollback.
Use Termination by choice to adaptively stop evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MGSM/MMLU, GuideEvolve reports 89.8%/89.1% accuracy versus Gödel Agent’s 90.6%/87.9%, 25–59% lower variance, 100% versus 82% evolution success, and 15.1/13.4 versus 30 optimization iterations.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover two benchmarks; expert-evaluation costs and robustness in production settings remain unclear from the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: GuideEvolve: Self-Evolving Agent Framework with Expert Guidance and 3Ts Mechanisms

title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
authors: M. Mikail Demir
abstract: Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.

infographic.key_insight: Decision models can match generative LLM accuracy at much lower cost while reducing—but not eliminating—unsupported legal citations when correct authority is missing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Use decision-model agreement to gate generative answers, and evaluate wrong citations alongside accuracy when building legal verification systems.
method: Replace the correct holding in 1,670 of 5,314 CaseHOLD items to test abstention.
Compare four probability-output decision models with six generative LLMs.
Test agreement-based gating and label-free probability distillation into Qwen3-8B.
infographic.evidence_signal: A decision model achieved 88.1% standard CaseHOLD accuracy versus the best generative LLM’s 88.2% at 1/55 of its cost; agreement gating halved that LLM’s wrong citations.
infographic.watch_item: Abstention remains imperfect: the most cautious decision model selected an incorrect option on 30% of missing-authority items, and broader legal settings need validation.
infographic.paper_title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority

title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration
authors: Sriyash Poddar, Yanda Bao, Jacob Krantz, Matthew Chang, Xavier Puig, Roozbeh Mottaghi
abstract: Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively. Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student--teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student's on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ~2x higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses ~100x fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by +40% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.

infographic.key_insight: ASTEROID teaches partially observed agents to explore by distilling a privileged expert’s actions on histories collected by the student itself.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a sample-efficient route to exploration policies for robotics and navigation, including vision-denied manipulation.
method: Collect on-policy interaction histories with a history-conditioned student under partial observability.
Use a privileged expert to label actions conditioned on the student’s collected context.
Train the student to search while uncertain and exploit once hidden task information is revealed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 11 environments, the abstract reports approximately 2× higher returns under fixed exploration budgets and 100× fewer interactions than RL baselines, plus a 40% success increase over standard distillation in real-world robot manipulation.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires a privileged expert capable of labeling student-visited contexts; obtaining such supervision may be difficult outside simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration

title: From Classifier Heads to Encoder Prototypes: Personalized Federated Learning with Head-Derived Clustering
authors: Amirardalan Dehghanpour, Arian Noori, Ehsan Tanghatari, Naimeh Omidvar, Hamid R. Rabiee
abstract: Personalized federated learning must decide which clients should share representations. We introduce HDC-FL (Head-Derived Clustering for Personalized Federated Learning), which reads that decision off a signal shared-encoder training already produces: the client-specific classifi- er heads. At periodic refresh rounds the server projects the cached heads into a normalized low-rank descriptor space, groups the descriptors, builds one encoder prototype per group from the cached client encoders, and returns to each client a soft mixture of those prototypes paired with its own unchanged head. Client-specific heads are never averaged or distributed to oth- er clients; the shared-encoder trajectory is left intact; and no second optimization trajectory, additional local objective, or post-training fine-tuning stage is required. Across 11 CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 configurations covering label-subset, Dirichlet and rotation heterogeneity with ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2 encoders, HDC-FL is competitive with the strongest personalized and clustered baselines in macro-averaged mean accuracy and attains the numerically highest macro-averaged worst-client and bottom-20% accuracy among the evaluated methods. The tail results distinguish methods that look similar when only their means are compared. A controlled donor-swap diagnostic further finds positive donor-ranking associations between head similarity and encoder compatibility in all three settings tested, most clearly under covariate shift.

infographic.key_insight: HDC-FL uses similarities between client-specific classifier heads to personalize encoder sharing, improving tail-client performance without averaging heads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method adds personalized encoder mixtures to shared-encoder training without a second optimization trajectory, an extra local objective, or post-training fine-tuning.
method: Periodically project cached classifier heads into normalized, low-rank descriptors and cluster clients.
Build one encoder prototype per cluster from cached client encoders.
Return a soft mixture of encoder prototypes to each client, paired with its own unchanged head.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 11 CIFAR-10/100 configurations with label-subset, Dirichlet, and rotation heterogeneity using ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2, HDC-FL achieves competitive macro-averaged mean accuracy and numerically highest macro-averaged worst-client and bottom-20% accuracy among evaluated methods.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the reported image-classification benchmarks; robustness of head-derived clusters in other tasks and deployment conditions remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: From Classifier Heads to Encoder Prototypes: Personalized Federated Learning with Head-Derived Clustering

title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
authors: Hanmin Li, Yury Demidovich, Peter Richtárik
abstract: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. Independent sets certify compatible edits whose verified gains, measured against the same current solution, add exactly. A coordinator constructs a safe compatible candidate and can also evaluate interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that an optimal fractional coloring yields a merger that preserves a $1/χ_f(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $χ_f(G)$ is the graph's fractional chromatic number. This guarantee is tight among mergers that select a subset of the same proposals. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost, yielding a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time-cost trade-off. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.

infographic.key_insight: Graph-compatible merging preserves at least 1/χ_f(G) of total verified local improvement, a tight guarantee for mergers selecting a subset of the same agent proposals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Dependency-aware coordination can prevent parallel agents from undoing one another’s gains while exposing trade-offs among task structure, agent allocation, time, and cost.
method: Model shared work as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph.
Verify edits against the same current solution and use independent sets to identify edits whose gains add exactly.
Use fractional coloring for guaranteed merging, optionally evaluate interacting edits, and optimize agent assignment via a linear program.
infographic.evidence_signal: Code-repair tests demonstrated conflict resolution; road-network tests retained 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs, while route-search scheduling reduced wall time by a median 15% across 12 paired runs.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require a known dependency graph and exact objective evaluation; geometric convergence additionally depends on local-improvement and block error-bound assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization

title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning
authors: Jingbo Wang, Kegeng Tang, Zihao Wang, Shaogang Ren
abstract: Causal discovery from nonlinear multivariate time series is challenging in high-dimensional systems, where the number of candidate directed relations grows quadratically with the number of variables. Existing methods are often limited by target-wise model fitting, repeated conditional testing, or expensive graph-search procedures. We propose SCDM, a shared-parameter meta-learning framework for scalable temporal causal discovery. SCDM treats each target variable as a task while learning a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix across tasks. Each meta-episode updates only a subset of target-variable tasks, allowing the model to accumulate structural evidence across the full system without exhaustive target-wise optimization. After training, a post-training graph readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores for threshold-independent evaluation. We also provide a finite-error recovery principle showing that, under fully observed delayed-system assumptions and a positive risk-gap condition, thresholding SCDM scores recovers the graph when statistical, meta-optimization, and readout errors are below the population margin. Experiments on controlled synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, high-dimensional, and real-world temporal benchmarks demonstrate competitive causal recovery and improved scalability in large temporal systems.

infographic.key_insight: SCDM scales causal discovery in nonlinear time series by sharing a temporal predictor and causal-strength matrix across target-variable tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Updating only a subset of targets per meta-episode reduces the need for exhaustive target-wise optimization in large temporal systems.
method: Treat each target variable as a task within a shared-parameter meta-learning framework.
Accumulate structural evidence through meta-episodes that update subsets of target tasks.
Convert the trained predictor into continuous directed causal scores using post-training graph readout.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on controlled synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, high-dimensional, and real-world temporal benchmarks report competitive causal recovery and improved scalability.
infographic.watch_item: The recovery guarantee requires fully observed delayed systems, a positive risk gap, and sufficiently small statistical, meta-optimization, and readout errors.
infographic.paper_title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning

title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Tianyi Lin, Wenxuan Liu
abstract: Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.

infographic.key_insight: Returning only optimal decisions can still expose a linear prediction model up to positive scaling, motivating a defense that perturbs decisions near decision boundaries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predict-then-optimize APIs should treat decision outputs as potential model-leakage channels and balance extraction resistance against optimization regret.
method: Establish sufficient conditions for recovering linear models from decision-only queries.
Construct an adaptive attack alternating inverse optimization with boundary-focused context queries.
Perturb decisions near cost-space decision boundaries, with regret and conditional extraction-error guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security–performance trade-off and show that the defense can increase extraction error.
infographic.watch_item: The extraction-error lower bound applies to attackers that fit defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, not necessarily all attack strategies.
infographic.paper_title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization

title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
authors: Zhennan Wan, Jianfei Chen
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: LongZero improves LLM long-context reasoning through self-generated tasks, without external training data or stronger teacher models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a way to reduce dependence on costly annotated datasets and external corpora when training long-context reasoning models.
method: Generate questions, answers, and supporting evidence in a compact structured form.
Expand the evidence into long multi-document contexts.
Train with GRPO on self-written multi-hop reasoning and multi-round retrieval tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two LLMs and five long-context reasoning benchmarks, the abstract reports generalization to real tasks and performance exceeding both baselines, including RL using externally sourced synthetic data.
infographic.watch_item: Self-generated answers and expanded evidence require consistency checks; the abstract does not quantify their reliability or training cost.
infographic.paper_title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data

title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback
authors: Meng Ding, Mingxi Lei, Jie Zhang, Jinyan Liu, Di Wang
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a central paradigm for aligning Large Language Models with human values. However, the reliance on sensitive preference data necessitates rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees to prevent user information leakage. Existing private alignment methods typically assume dense reward parameterizations, resulting in estimation error bounds that scale polynomially with the ambient {model size $d$}. Such dependence is prohibitive in modern {overparameterized models} where $d$ is vast. In this work, we study \emph{Private Sparse RLHF} problem to address this limitation, assuming that human preferences (reward model) are governed by a subset of $s^* \ll d$ relevant features. We provide the first comprehensive theoretical framework for differentially private sparse reward estimation from pairwise preference feedback under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, and introduce efficient algorithms for both Sample-DP and Label-DP settings. Theoretically, under the squared $\ell_2$ parameter estimation error, we establish upper bounds of $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + {s^*}^2/n^2\varepsilon^2)$ for $(\varepsilon,δ)$-Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + s^*/n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon$-Label-DP based on randomized response, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that the guarantee for our Label-DP method cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for the problem with Label-DP. Empirically, our framework demonstrates superior efficacy over dense baselines across sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks, offering a significantly more favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse reward estimation can make private RLHF error depend on the number of relevant features s* rather than polynomially on the full model dimension d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For high-dimensional reward models with sparse preference structure, this approach offers a potentially better privacy–utility trade-off than dense private estimation.
method: Model pairwise preferences using Bradley–Terry–Luce with an s*-sparse reward parameter.
Develop Sample-DP and randomized-response Label-DP estimators.
Prove squared parameter-error bounds of Õ(s*/n + s*²/(n²ε²)) for Sample-DP and Õ(s*/n + s*/(nε²)) for Label-DP.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks report better privacy–utility trade-offs than dense baselines; the abstract provides no numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits rely on sparse reward structure, and Label-DP protects preference labels rather than entire training records.
infographic.paper_title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback

title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
authors: Xinzhe Wang, Xudong Weng, Zang Li, Shaolei Zhang
abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

infographic.key_insight: Charts can serve as internal reasoning actions for data agents, but agents need experience-based guidance—not just plotting access—to use them effectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Data-analysis agents can improve analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality by learning when to use text, charts, or both without updating model parameters.
method: Probe chart use with 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions.
Distil rollout experience into guidance for analytical operations and evidence-format selection.
Judge outcomes and intermediate steps, admitting only experience that improves held-out validation performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three held-out benchmarks and four LLM backbones, the method improves accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines; charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no effect sizes or runtime costs, leaving the practical trade-off between gains and added rollout, judging, and validation overhead unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis

title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
authors: Mohammed Saqlain
abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

infographic.key_insight: Retrieval is the main bottleneck in biomedical claim verification: valid PubMed IDs can still point to irrelevant papers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Scientific-agent harnesses should enable model-written search queries and validate citation relevance, not merely identifier existence.
method: Evaluate SciFact claim verification with live PubMed as the only tool.
Compare closed-book, claim-as-query retrieval, ReAct-style search, and gold-abstract oracle harnesses.
Hold output format fixed and test each harness with two efficient frontier backbones.
infographic.evidence_signal: Agent-written queries tripled gold-paper recall over naive retrieval and achieved 62% verdict accuracy; gold abstracts raised accuracy to 79–86%, while only 3 of 327 existing closed-book citations were judged relevant.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy differences among realistic harnesses were not statistically significant at this sample size, and agents used less than half their search budget.
infographic.paper_title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents

title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
authors: Matteo Benati, Alessandro Londei, Denise Lanzieri, Raffaello Mastromarino, Vittorio Loreto
abstract: Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

infographic.key_insight: Dreaming Learning mitigates model collapse by training on high-temperature self-generated samples that counteract the loss of diversity caused by low-temperature sampling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For generative models trained recursively on synthetic data, an auxiliary dreaming loss may help preserve diversity when data accumulation alone does not stop collapse.
method: Track collapse through the eigenvalue spectrum of a learned Markov transition operator.
Add an auxiliary loss on model-generated samples drawn at dreaming temperature T_d > 1.
Counter low-temperature sharpening to keep transition probabilities from vanishing and eigenvalues away from the unit circle.
infographic.evidence_signal: Spectral measurements over 5,000 generations support the mechanism, with mitigation also observed in LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.
infographic.watch_item: The spectral mechanism is studied in a controlled Markov setting; effectiveness and temperature tuning require validation for larger models and deployment data.
infographic.paper_title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
